Antiparallel

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: a circle through two corners of a triangle draws a line across the other two sides.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or the circle's centre P, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Tick "Equal angles" to see why the new line matches the angles of the triangle.
Look for the math

Drag the corners and watch the green line. Its ends move, yet it always meets the two sides of the triangle at the same angles as the bottom side does — in the opposite order. That is why it is called an antiparallel.

Parallel and antiparallel

Two parallel lines meet a transversal at equal angles in the same positions. Here the two lines are angled the other way around: the angle that AB makes with one side equals the angle that DE makes with the other. Drag P and the green chord keeps this reversed match, even when one of its ends lies beyond a corner.

The circle makes the chord

P is kept on the perpendicular bisector of AB, so its circle passes through A and B. It meets BC again at D and AC again at E, and the chord DE is drawn through them. All four points A, B, D and E lie on that one circle: they form a cyclic quadrilateral. Moving P changes the size of the circle, and so slides D and E along the sides; moving A or B moves P with them at the same distance from AB.

Opposite angles and the reversed order

When D and E both fall on the sides of the triangle, ABDE is convex. Its opposite angles add to 180°. Taking the supplementary angles at D and E turns that statement into the equality of the two pairs of angles shown by the coloured arcs. Inscribed angles say the same thing another way: ∠ADB and ∠AEB are equal or supplementary, because both stand on the chord AB.

What the checks found

The logic test tries nine named triangles and 220 generated ones, with the centre on either side of AB. In every well-cut case the two angle pairs match to within a millionth of a radian, D and E lie on the circle and on their lines, the inscribed angles are equal or supplementary, and — when both cuts are on the sides — the opposite angles add to 180°. It also rebuilds the whole construction from the old applet's bytecode and gets the same D and E. The old article now embeds a GeoGebra drawing instead of the Java applet, but its text describes exactly the construction used here.

Try dragging P far below AB: one cut jumps past a corner, and the reversed angle match still holds.
